title: Example: the gamut window
lead: An example of InkProf’s ICC-derived colour volume in a separate window.
images: Figure 6. InkProf’s gamut view using an example sRGB profile (ICC v2). sRGB illustrates the window; this is not a measured printer gamut.
sections: Read the axes and surface

L* represents lightness. a* runs from green to red, b* from blue to yellow. The surface is calculated from the profile’s colour transform in CIELAB D50. Rotate the view in the app; the PDF image is static.
Use the view as supporting information

A larger surface is not itself a quality score. Assess measurements, colour errors and real prints. In a printer project, Select area chooses regions for manual reinforcement with additional measured samples. See page 56.

title: Two stages of regularization
sections: Stage 1: Measurement data smoothing

Choose Off, Argyll colprof model or an InkProf-owned model. Pre-regularization creates separate derived input before the final ICC. Original spectra, XYZ and raw measurements remain preserved. The feature is experimental and off by default.
Argyll: Assumed noise (%)
The first colprof model uses an assumed average deviation through -r, normally 0.5%. This is not an exact measured Delta E00. The model is evaluated at the original RGB values.
Stage 2: Smoothing at ICC build
This controls final colprof -r. Empty uses 0.5%. The value is independent of the first-stage noise assumption. Percentages display one decimal without rounding stored precision.
FWA/OBA and B1

New B2 recipes support native M0 FWA before Argyll pre-smoothing and final fitting. Compensation is applied once, not again to derived XYZ. Changing FWA preserves B1 but requires new B2 and later results. See the M0 white-reference section.

title: Test RGB gradients
sections: B2 selection and Manual B3

With pre-regularization selected, tick Open RGB gradient test after profile build. The window opens after successful Manual B3. Save recipe in B2 does not start the check. Automatic B3 creates its own recipes and does not use this B2 choice.
Run RGB check

Nine RGB paths with 1,025 samples each are evaluated through the final ICC. Select a path and relative or perceptual intent. Curves show RGB, Lab, adjacent Delta E00 steps and Lab second differences. JSON and Markdown are saved in the job's checks folder.
Check blue-sky inverse
The blue-sky test uses B2A and returns through A2B. It complements the forward check and changes neither recipe nor ICC. Reopen a closed window with inkprof.checkRGBGradients(jobFolder).
Interpretation

Large local steps, reversals and second differences identify places to investigate. Real printer curvature can also produce these values. No universal pass threshold is used. Printed gradients and documented viewing conditions are needed for physical assessment.

title: Remeasure a whole printed row
sections: New measurement or earlier revision

Measure starts a new measurement. Saved revisions selects an earlier saved revision. Import file reads an external file. For isolated problems, use Remeasure patch or Remeasure row in the overview. A new save preserves previous history.
Select page and row

Remeasure row uses the printed page and row number. B24 means position B, row 24; patch ID is separate. Original scan mode, tolerance and instrument conditions are retained. An isolated session measures only the selected row.
Measure and review

Click Measure selected row, calibrate and follow FORWARD/REVERSE. Save supplies candidate values. Change Delta E00 compares previous and new measurements, not error against desired colour. Accept row replacement creates a revision replacing only this row. Discard / Close retains previous values.
Preserved traceability

Original data, new raw readings and the decision are saved. Old paired readings are labelled historical after row replacement. Select and review the correct workflow revision before locking B1 again; Accept in the remeasurement window does not necessarily select profiling input.

title: C2: profile, TIFF and print chain
sections: Conversion and tag

Lab-based targets use B2A, absolute colorimetry and BPC off. Layout and RGB16 quantization follow. The exact printer ICC is now embedded as a tag without another pixel conversion. Earlier exports do not change when code is updated.
Keep already converted values

When opening in Photoshop, discard/ignore the embedded profile without converting RGB values; do not convert to a working space. Print at 100% without further colour conversion. Assigned sRGB or Adobe RGB followed by conversion can greatly change older untagged targets. Read PRINTING.txt and document the chain.
Contents and difficult colours

The profiling-workflow default is 80 colours, 24 neutrals, 12 challenges and 12 repeats. Counts can be changed. Challenges may be outside gamut or have an unresolved inverse. C2 therefore does not contain only previous problem colours.
White margin

An unprinted margin uses pure device RGB white. A white image area converted with absolute intent may receive colour to reproduce the reference white point. This is not the paper's own whiteness. A converted image margin and the target background are therefore different things.

title: Read the C3 table and warnings
sections: Identity and Lab

Page and Coordinate identify position. ID is identity and Role is patch type. Desired Lab is desired colour; Measured Lab is the print. L* is lightness, negative/positive a* green/red and negative/positive b* blue/yellow.
Two error columns

Measured vs desired (dE00) compares measurement with desired colour. Model vs measurement (dE00) compares ICC prediction with measurement. Similar numbers do not mean similar colours: if both are large, measurement differs from both. Near zero in the second column means close model agreement.
Sorting and groups

Largest errors appear first. Main statistics include unique patches, including challenges, but not extra repeats. Filter groups before drawing conclusions. Small differences between repeats or forward/reverse show repeatability, not accuracy.
Suspected double colour management

C3 simulates extra conversion from sRGB and Adobe RGB to the printer profile and warns when a simulation explains measurements much better. This is a hypothesis; other print faults may look similar. Check assignment, conversion and the driver before retraining the model.

title: Reference colours and an existing ICC
sections: Fixed reference set

C2 can use a Lab table, Argyll CIE/CGATS with Lab or XYZ, or TI1 with device RGB. Use only material you are entitled to use. Names and patch codes are preserved for C3. A reference name does not imply protected vendor layout or data are included.
Lab or RGB

Lab references are converted through the ICC and test inverse, print and measurement together. Device RGB is printed as given without ICC conversion; reference Lab is the A2B prediction. PRINTING.txt and verification.json identify the method.
New project: Verify existing ICC

The separate seven-step workflow imports RGB printer profiles in ICC v2 and v4, creates a target, measures, analyses, reviews, records assessment and saves a certificate. The original colour tables are used and delivered. V4.4 is checked natively through LittleCMS; verification does not use a v2 reconstruction. The 575-patch suggestion covers skin tones, shadows, neutrals and broad colours.
Unknown independence

If original training data are unavailable, independence is unknown. Numerical checks and a good photographic impression do not give automatic approval or ISO certification. Document intended use, the chain and limitations.
Methods in RGB Target

The RGB target designer offers OFPS, incremental far point, quasi-random, body-centred cubic and random through Argyll. An existing ICC can guide patch placement but is not measurement data. Argyll preconditioning with v4 needs a separate, explicitly accepted approximate v2 copy; the original is preserved.

title: Diagnose with JSON and the right check
sections: Traceable chain

B1 locks measurement input. The job saves recipe.json, status.json and result/profile.icc. C2 saves an exact ICC copy, desired Lab, RGB16 and placement in verification.json. C3 links measurement JSON and its TI3 revision through hashes. Coordinate and ID are different identifiers.
Built-in MATLAB checks

inkprof.checkProfileFit checks the forward model against training. inkprof.checkProfileGrid and inkprof.checkProfileC1 provide grid, CMM and inverse diagnostics. inkprof.checkVerificationTarget compares the verification print. inkprof.checkRGBGradients opens the gradient window. Read each check's purpose.
Separate scripts are not app buttons

The development measurement-JSON inverse script compared Lab, inverse RGB and return through A2B. It is not a built-in InkProf function. Small Lab-RGB-Lab error shows internal consistency, not a correct physical print. Alternative solutions can give large RGB differences.
Test the hypothesis first

First check suspected wrong ICC or inverse numerically and through hashes, without another print. Check a suspected wrong row against TI2 and by remeasurement. A changed print chain may require a new sample with identical device RGB. Do not rebuild the model to conceal an unresolved chain error.

title: Compare accuracy and gradients
sections: Open the comparison

After valid B1, choose Compare accuracy and gradients in the main window. Enter one to six positive final colprof -r values. Compare the currently offered Argyll candidates.  Several builds may take minutes; progress is displayed.
Read the results

Compare fit against original measurements, held-out evidence where available, model change and photographic-gradient diagnostics. Training fit is not independent validation. Inspect matching gradient paths: an average across different interior coverage can mislead.
Automatic B3 selection

With development controls, Automatic tests final -r values 0.5, 1 and 1.5 at high table quality. Selection balances accuracy and float-gradient smoothness. Guards check patch and gray regressions, curvature, reversals, coverage and colour span. Defaults permit 0.05 RMS accuracy tradeoff for at least 5% gradient improvement. These are numerical selection rules, not print acceptance criteria. Without development controls, one candidate is built with no claim of superiority.
Choose deliberately

Comparison preserves B1 and leaves the current workflow ICC selected. To use a comparison setting, enter it in B2 and build Manual B3. New recipes support FWA before pre-smoothing with the measured-white requirements described in the M0 section.

title: Photographic gradient conversion
sections: Open the diagnostic

Choose Photographic gradients in the main window after a successful profile build, or in the RGB gradient window. The check uses the exact selected ICC and saves JSON and Markdown in its checks folder.
What is tested

Nine paths with 1,025 samples are converted from sRGB and Adobe RGB (1998) to printer RGB, then through relative A2B to predicted Lab. Relative and perceptual intent, BPC on/off, and float, 16-bit and 8-bit input/output buffers give 216 combinations. LittleCMS performs these conversions; Photoshop and printer drivers may behave differently.
Read the columns

Curvature P95 measures normalized Lab second differences. L* reversals count decreasing lightness steps on eligible interior points; interpret them in relation to the chosen path. Unique RGB codes and unchanged steps describe quantization plateaus. The JSON also records longest plateau and Lab span. Large numbers are not automatically visible defects.
Limits of the test

Hard device clipping is excluded from comparison metrics, but this is not a proven physical-gamut mask. Quantization plateaus are expected, especially at 8 bit. Compare matching paths and precision. Numerical smoothness does not certify absence of banding; verify printed gradients.

title: Certificate evidence
sections: Pre-regularization in the certificate

The certificate records the selected job recipe, pre-regularization method, its assumed noise (avgdev) and final colprof -r. Saved results include the model change when available. Raw measurements are preserved. Model change is not print accuracy. The former InkProf grid regularization and its measurement weights have been removed.
Gradient evidence and regeneration

A saved photographic-gradient report is included only if its SHA-256 matches the certificate ICC. The certificate summarizes CMM, settings, sample count, interior coverage, reversals and curvature, and embeds full per-path evidence in JSON. Missing evidence is stated explicitly. Re-run step 14 for a new certificate; historical and signed certificates are preserved.

title: One ICC, three rendering intents
sections: New B2 recipes

Newly built profiles support perceptual, relative colorimetric and absolute colorimetric in one ICC file. B2 provides Perceptual compression (%), passed to colprof -s. The default 20% generic compression is a starting setting, not a measured optimum. Automatic B3 carries forward this B2 value.
What the ICC contains

Perceptual uses a gamut-mapped B2A0 table. Relative uses B2A1. Absolute uses the relative table plus the media white point (wtpt); it does not require a separate B2A3 table. The colour-management application selects the rendering intent. The profile header default does not prevent choosing another intent.
Build validation and certificate

New builds require perceptual and relative tables with distinct data and a valid media-white tag before publication. Saved jobs and certificates record the rendering-intent settings. Structural validation and numerical conversions do not establish print quality.
Update an existing profile

Restart InkProf, save a new B2 recipe and rebuild B3 to obtain the new gamut mapping. Existing recipes, ICC files and imported profiles are preserved. Recheck the profile and its print before approval and delivery. C2 verification still applies the ICC once, absolute without BPC, followed by printing with colour management disabled.

title: ICC v2 or v4.4: which fits best?
lead: Choose according to the printing application, rendering intent and checked results. A higher version number does not itself make a profile more colour-accurate.
sections: What v4 adds
ICC v4 clarifies the reference colour space and rendering intents for more predictable interpretation across profiles and engines. It does not replace good measurements or print assessment.
When v2 is a good choice
Keep v2 in a working, checked workflow, particularly for older applications or recipients requiring it. InkProf uses v2 internally for Argyll. Do not switch solely for a higher version number.
When v4.4 is a good choice

Choose v4.4 when the application and recipient support it and the result has been assessed. InkProf preserves colorimetric tables but remaps perceptual and saturation tables. Shadows and transitions may change; improvement is not guaranteed.
Both for comparison

Both gives both versions from the same profiling run. Compare the same photograph, gradients and shadows with the same paper, ink, settings, intent and viewing light. Record BPC and change one part of the chain at a time.
Numerical BPC example

Two profiles were tested through LittleCMS at sRGB greys 0, 8, 32, 128 and 255. Perceptual v4.4 gave identical results with BPC on and off; predicted L* differed by at most 0.79 from v2 with BPC on. This is a numerical example, not a new print measurement or general guarantee.
What verification establishes

C2 uses absolute colorimetry without BPC. A good result does not establish your preferred perceptual rendering. The certificate identifies the checked profile and v4.4 conversion separately. Also assess a print using the production version and intent.
Import and the practical decision

InkProf imports RGB printer profiles in v2 and v4. Existing v4 verification uses the original through LittleCMS. Argyll preconditioning requires an accepted approximate v2 copy. Choose according to your chain, measurements and image assessment.
links: ICC: reasons for changing to v4

title: TIFF: conversion versus embedded ICC
sections: Read the companion text file

PRINTING.txt beside modern TIFF targets, and *-README.txt for the legacy exporter, list ICC conversion and Embedded ICC separately. Tagged files identify the printer profile and its SHA-256. C2 also has package-level PRINTING.txt; read it together with print/PRINTING.txt.
Conversion: what changed the pixels?

Base and refinement targets render source device RGB directly without a printer ICC conversion by InkProf. Ordinary C2 colour-reference targets have already passed through the printer ICC once, absolute colorimetric without BPC. C2 device-RGB reference sets instead print their RGB unchanged; the ICC predicts reference Lab only. Imported source history may be unknown.
Tag: what identifies the file?

Both kinds of C2 TIFF embed the printer ICC as an identifying tag. Embedding alone changes no pixels and is not an instruction to apply the ICC again. A tag does not prove that no other conversion occurred earlier. InkProf records its own processing separately. Base and refinement targets normally have no embedded profile.
Print without another conversion

Print at 100% with colour management disabled in the application, OS print path and driver. Preserve any embedded tag without conversion. Do not assign another profile or convert the TIFF to a working space. A program can use the embedded tag if colour management is enabled. New packages contain the clearer instructions; existing TIFFs and packages are preserved.

title: Appendix: workflow diagram
lead: Overview of the example on the following pages: from planning to measured final verification and saved delivery.
sections: Using the feedback loop

When results deviate, first review measurements, profile identity and print settings. Refine only when supported by evidence; otherwise investigate or withhold approval. A new ICC requires fresh final verification. The diagram shows the print-verified route, not the separate numerical delivery route.

title: Appendix: plan and create the base target
sections: 1. Define success before printing

Agree on photographic use or a specific reference condition, viewing light, important colours and gradients, and acceptance criteria. Record printer, ink, paper, driver preset, quality, resolution, backing and instrument. Check nozzles and allow consistent drying time. A custom RGB target does not establish ISO proofing conformity.
2. Use an existing ICC as a starting estimate

Choose a reliable RGB printer ICC for the same printer, ink, paper and settings, or a reasonably similar system. In target generation, select an Argyll method supporting perceptual placement and supply the preconditioning profile. Argyll uses its predictions to distribute device-RGB patches; the base target is not converted through that ICC. A poor or unrelated profile can bias sampling. Without a suitable ICC, use an unconditioned initial target and improve the sampling after the first build.
3. Choose the measurement budget

A practical starting recommendation is about 1,000 colour samples with broad RGB coverage, neutrals, shadows, skin tones and distributed controls. For a careful full profile, 1,500–2,000 samples are reasonable; the existing 2,000-patch route is appropriate when measurement time permits. A 300–600-sample pilot can reveal setup problems before a larger run. These are workflow recommendations, not a universal optimum or a software default. Reserve space for repeats and several unprinted-white readings; confirm the actual generated count, including controls, in the preview.
Decision before saving

Preserve patch size and instrument scan geometry. Choose paper dimensions and inspect the actual page preview. Save the TIFF16 together with its matching TI2, layout and PRINTING.txt. Keep the original ICC and its identity with the project. A target-generation preconditioner is distinct from the profile later built from the measurements.

title: Appendix: print, measure and decide on OBA
sections: 4. Print the prepared RGB target

Follow its PRINTING.txt. In the Photoshop profile-mismatch dialog choose Discard the embedded profile (don’t color manage). Disable colour management in the printing application and colour adjustment in the driver. Print at 100% with the recorded preset. Do not convert to Adobe RGB or apply the printer ICC again. An identifying embedded ICC does not change this instruction. C2 reference targets have already received their specified preparation; their RGB values must also reach the printer unchanged.
5. Measure and review before B1

Calibrate the instrument, use consistent backing and scan direction, and measure all pages. Save each measurement round as a revision. Review identities, white controls, duplicate colours and unusual readings; remeasure suspect patches or a whole row with the correct page and forward/reverse choice. Correct acquisition errors before smoothing. Select and accept the intended revision, then lock B1. Keep different print rounds identifiable.
6. Decide whether FWA/OBA compensation is needed

Do not enable compensation solely because white looks yellow or a UV lamp makes the paper glow. Consider the paper, verified measurement condition and intended viewing light. For the supported i1Pro2 M0 route, compensation is a D50 simulation using available visible spectra, not a measurement of UV excitation or an M1 result. If the paper has little OBA, or the available evidence does not support compensation, retain the uncompensated route and document the choice.
If compensation is selected

Use native M0 spectra with verified instrument metadata and sufficient spectral coverage. InkProf averages available white-patch spectra and records their count and variation. If no usable white reference exists, B2 offers blank-paper measurement, a saved approved reference, or Cancel. Measure several clean locations on the same paper with the same backing. Averaging can reduce random noise; it cannot recover missing excitation information. Save a new B2 recipe. Keep compensation and viewing assumptions consistent through comparisons and final verification; changing this choice invalidates later results.

title: Appendix: build, refine and stop
sections: 7. Choose smoothing and the B3 route

Start with Argyll only (raw measurements) when repeatability is good. If noisy measurements or gradients justify it, compare Argyll colprof pre-smoothing (experimental) against the raw route. Its Assumed noise (%) and Smoothing at ICC build are separate settings; 0.5% is the initial recipe value, not an established optimum for every instrument. Check colour fit and equivalent photographic gradient paths. Select the RGB gradient test when useful. For an exact saved B2 recipe, choose Manual in B3; Automatic creates its own recipes and does not inherit every B2 smoothing setting. With FWA and pre-smoothing, use the newly saved supported two-pass recipe.
8. Select the refinement method

Use Argyll only as the initial refinement choice: Argyll places additional patches using the current profile. Current InkProf (Jacobian sampling) uses measured local residuals and local response to propose additional RGB samples. Both routes build the resulting ICC with Argyll. Choose Jacobian sampling when a reproducible local discrepancy warrants targeted investigation; do not expect it to make unattainable colours printable. Save the choice with the proposal. Print and measure the added device-RGB target unchanged, then build the next iteration.
9. Compare equivalent evidence

Use row 18 for Previous profile prediction vs current profile prediction at common samples. Separately review fitting error, development/held-out evidence where available, repeatability, gradients and Measured print vs desired colour. A smaller training error alone is insufficient. A small inverse round-trip error only shows consistency of the model and inverse. Large measured discrepancies require checks of profile identity, RGB values, print management, patch mapping and measurement conditions before attributing them to gamut.
10. Decide whether another iteration is worthwhile

Continue when a specific measured uncertainty can be reduced. Stop when comparable errors and gradients show no useful improvement beyond repeatability, or a further round produces an unacceptable accuracy/smoothness trade-off. One or two comparable rounds without meaningful gain are a practical review trigger, not an automatic InkProf acceptance rule. Record the evidence, selected profile and reason for stopping. Numerical convergence does not prove physical colour accuracy or compliance.

title: Appendix: final verification and certificate
sections: 11. Verify the exact profile to be delivered

After choosing the final iteration, run row 8 (Fit, Grid and C1) and row 9 (C2: save verification TIFF16) for that current profile. Make a new control print with the documented settings and no further colour conversion. Measure it in row 10, retain the revision, and run row 11 (C3) and row 12 (feedback). Do this even if development or training measurements already look good. A measurement used to train a later build cannot independently verify that later ICC.
12. Assess the whole result

Review count, mean, median, P95 and maximum for all assessed unique colours, not only the worst patches. Identify challenge colours, controls and repeatability. Compare desired-colour error with current-profile prediction error where available. Inspect important photographs and gradients. Model-reachable, outside-model/inversion-unresolved and unclassified references describe model evidence; they are not proof of a physical gamut limit. Confirm white, black, neutral balance and the intended viewing conditions.
13. Approve or decline the intended use

In row 13, enter review notes, scope, print settings, limitations and the decision. Approval is justified only by the relevant measured evidence and agreed criteria. If a required standard limit is not met, report it; printer limitations do not waive that requirement. Photographic use may be approved with explicit limitations when agreed, while conformity for a different use is declined. If the remaining cause is unresolved, say so. Row 14 exports the selected ICC and English measurement certificate.
14. Preserve the evidence and status

Check that the certificate identifies this ICC, iteration, current verification revision, regularisation, FWA reference and reviewer decision. Retain the target, TI2/layout, PRINTING.txt, raw measurements, recipe, ICC and complete reports. Row 19 is numerical-only delivery and cannot replace fresh measured verification. If the ICC or print setup changes after approval, repeat final verification. The defensible conclusion is measured and approved for the stated use, with disclosed limits—not automatic ISO approval.

title: Appendix: evidence behind the recommendations
sections: Argyll: sampling and measurement quality

The targen documentation supports using a prior or similar ICC to guide perceptual patch placement. printtarg explains instrument-dependent patch geometry and randomised locations, which help identification and distribute spatial printing effects. Preserve the generated layout; do not rearrange patches manually. There is no universally optimal patch count. The suggested budgets in this appendix are InkProf working recommendations to be evaluated against repeatability and independent results.
Argyll: smoothing is an uncertainty assumption

colprof defines -r as the assumed average deviation of device and instrument readings, with a default of 0.5%. Raising it gives less weight to individual readings and more to collective behaviour. A percentage is not ΔE00. Estimate the need from repeat readings and compare accuracy and gradients; do not increase smoothing simply to conceal a systematic print error.
X-Rite: distinguish M0 compensation from M1

X-Rite describes M1 as the preferred condition for OBA-enhanced substrates and explains that M0 does not fully define UV content. The i1Pro2 hardware supports M1, but the InkProf path described here uses verified M0 data. Recording spectral bands near or below 400 nm does not measure the illumination spectrum or establish calibrated UV excitation. Averaging white readings improves repeatability, not the physical definition of M0. Use actual M1 measurements in a compatible workflow when required by the reference or conformity claim.
Fogra: verification needs the relevant reference and control

Fogra links contract-proof verification to its defined MediaWedge, printing condition and applicable tolerances. An InkProf custom RGB verification and reviewer approval are useful evidence for a stated use, but do not substitute for that complete procedure. The independent final control print in this appendix is an InkProf quality-control recommendation.
What external sources do not establish

These sources do not demonstrate that InkProf Jacobian sampling outperforms Argyll only, nor that the recommended patch budgets or stopping triggers are universally optimal. Those decisions require comparable local results. Sources reviewed on 8 October 2026; the handbook describes current InkProf behaviour separately from external guidance.

title: Appendix: comparing profiling methods
sections: A photographic starting point

Torger recommends preconditioning, optimised placement and extra greys. His Colormunki example favours about 840 patches as a practical balance; this is experience with that instrument and print system, not a universal limit. He uses colprof -r1.0 to trade a little fit accuracy for smoothness and evaluates diagnostic gradients and a familiar photograph. His reported profile-matching errors compare predictions with measured device patches, including training-data checks; they are not interchangeable with InkProf C3 errors against desired colours on a separate profile-converted print. His tutorial is primarily a base-profiling workflow, not evidence that InkProf refinement replicates a particular iterative algorithm.
A more extensive measurement workflow

X-Rite’s recommended RGB workflow proposes 2,033 or 1,586 patches, wider patches for better sampling, about an hour of drying, instrument calibration and saved measurement data. These recommendations concern its own software and layouts: do not blindly increase InkProf patch width or assume one hour guarantees stability for every paper. i1Profiler also offers targeted optimisation and optical-brightener compensation; the internal engine is not Argyll, and its OBC must not be described as identical to InkProf’s M0 method.
Reconciled recommendation for InkProf

For a paper used regularly and a careful i1Pro2 profiling job, begin with approximately 1,500–2,000 patches when feasible. Around 800–1,000 is a reasonable lower-budget start; a 300–600-patch pilot is for setup checks. Use a suitable existing ICC for placement, distribute neutral and white controls, and preserve reliable patch geometry. Compare raw Argyll fitting with justified smoothing on the same data. Choose further patches from measured evidence rather than a fixed obligation to iterate.
The final decision remains measured

Neither an attractive photograph nor low model-fit error alone establishes measured accuracy for the intended reference. Keep the familiar photographic check and gradient review, then make the independent final C2 print and C3 measurement before reviewer approval and certificate delivery. This combines practical photographic assessment with traceable measurement.

title: Test images
sections: Photographic test images

Keith Cooper (Northlight Images) provides printer test images and assessment notes, including the Datacolor image made available courtesy of Datacolor. Use it for overall photographic assessment of skin tones, neutrals, shadows and saturated colours. In InkProf comparisons, inspect the sky gradient for banding or uneven transitions when assessing smoothing; it is a visual diagnostic, not proof of a particular cause. Compare the same source, ICC path, intent, BPC, print preset and viewing light. The original Adobe RGB photograph needs one intended printer-profile conversion; an already converted device-RGB version must receive no second conversion. Do not apply fitting-target opening instructions to the original photograph. JPEG quantisation and clipping can also produce visible steps; use synthetic high-precision gradients alongside it. Download from Keith Cooper’s page; the image is not distributed in the InkProf repository.

title: Manual gamut reinforcement
lead: Manually strengthen measurement coverage in a chosen colour region. You choose where more samples are needed; refinement requires printing, measurement and a new profile build.
sections: 1. Check the current profile
Rows 7 and 8 (C1. Fit, Grid and C1) must show Complete. Row 15 requires current numerical checks. If it is Locked, complete row 8 and click Refresh.
2. Select the region manually

Open View gamut. Use Rotate view to expose the region, then Select area in the right panel. Click the coloured surface; a white marker identifies the selection. Choose several points around an indentation if needed. Clear selection removes all markers.
3. Review and save the samples

Defaults: Neighbour radius 3 RGB percentage points, Minimum spacing 1, Maximum new patches 100. Click Review patches / create TIFF16, uncheck unwanted rows, then Create TIFF16 target. Existing training colours and near duplicates are excluded. Extra controls increase the printed total.
4. Choose paper and close the gamut view

Review the paper suggestion. Preview selected dimensions opens a temporary preview. Close it with the red window button, then click Use these dimensions behind it to save. Close the gamut window after saving; it stays open until you close it.
5. Link the selection to row 15

Select row 15 and Run selected step. Choose From gamut selection and Use latest selection. Record your reason and confirm the paper dimensions. Wait for Complete. This saves the workflow print package, including pending C2 colours when applicable.
6. Print, measure and rebuild

Select row 15 and "Copy TIFF16 for printing…". Print this package at 100% with colour management disabled and the same printer, paper and settings. Let it dry. Run row 16, Measure refinement, then row 17, Build next iteration. Assess the new profile with a fresh independent verification print.
callout: Manual supplementation is not automatic error detection. Printer RGB is approximately associated with the selected vertex through forward ICC samples. ΔE76 offset is the association distance, not measured print error. More measurements may strengthen the model, but cannot extend physical gamut or guarantee that an indentation disappears.

tag: BEFORE STRIP MEASUREMENT | RGB PRINT CHECK
title: Catch incorrect print settings early
lead: InkProf checks the RGB squares on new pages before the long strip measurement starts. A large difference from an approved print can stop an incorrectly configured print after just a few spot readings.
sections: 1. Check settings even with Photoshop presets

A saved Adobe Photoshop preset is not proof that the current print uses the correct settings. Check colour management in Photoshop and the printer driver, media type, resolution and other project conditions before every print. Base targets and already prepared C2/refinement targets must not receive an extra ICC conversion. Follow the target printing instructions.
2. Measure the three controls before the strips

Each new TIFF16 page has red, green and blue 8 × 8 mm squares below the profiling grid. Select Start measurement. InkProf starts with the RGB check: calibrate as instructed and hold i1 Pro 2 stationary at the centre of each square with the same backing. Select Measure square; do not swipe. The check uses native M0. Follow the displayed page and R, G or B.
3. Approve a known-correct print as the reference

The first check needs a print whose paper and colour settings you have independently checked. After the spot readings, select Approve as print reference. InkProf saves the RGB values as the project reference. Without an approved reference, pages are compared with page 1; this cannot detect a shared error on all pages. Changed recorded printer, paper or print conditions require a new reference.
4. Failed or a reasoned override

Above the default 5 ΔE00 threshold, strip measurement is stopped and the step receives Failed. Page, colour and difference are saved. Check active print settings and reprint if needed. To accept the difference anyway, select Override…, enter your reason and select Save override and continue. The reason, date and original values are retained; the reference and threshold are unchanged. Missing readings cannot be bypassed.
Separate from profiling; older pages still work

Control squares do not affect profile fitting. Older targets without declared RGB controls are measured as before and are not rejected for missing squares. Recorded Paper finish, such as Matte, is retained with the check. Compare matte papers with a correct reference for the same paper; a smaller gamut does not itself mean a larger difference from that reference. Paper type and reasoned exceptions may inform future thresholds, but the threshold does not change automatically.

title: From verification target to an approved certificate
lead: A good measurement result is not a saved approval. Verify the current ICC, record your assessment and then export the certificate.
sections: 1. Row 9: choose a target for the current profile

Run row 9. Choose Create new target, then Default or Other file for ColorChecker (a Lab file, not an image), or Generated balanced set for broader control coverage. 12 extra repeats means 12 extra patches. For an already printed ColorChecker, choose Select existing target; see page 59.
2. Print the saved TIFF16 target

Print at 100% size with the recorded paper and settings. Lab references have already been converted through the ICC once. Do not apply another colour conversion in Photoshop or the driver. Check active settings even with presets. Allow the print to dry. Page 57 describes the RGB check before strip measurement.
3. Row 10: measure the correct print and save

Run row 10 and choose Measure for a new measurement. Check the target name and patch count in Confirm measurement target before choosing Measure this target. Save and finish saves the measurement. Saved revisions selects an already saved measurement of the same target. Previous files remain when the C2 selection changes.
4. Rows 11 and 12: compare and review

Run C3. Compare model and print, then Review feedback. Assess measured errors, grays, repeats and out-of-gamut colours. Approve only for the use and requirements supported by the results. Evidence from an older target or profile does not replace verification of the current ICC.
5. Row 13: save your explicit approval

Run Approve for intended use. Enter intended use, quality requirements and accepted limitations in Your assessment. Tick the confirmation that you reviewed the results and checked print settings against the project. Select Approve for stated use. Example: Approved for photographic prints on the stated paper after ColorChecker verification. Measured colour errors and stated limitations are accepted for this use. Adapt the text to your actual assessment.
6. Row 14: export the certificate

Run Save ICC and measurement certificate. The certificate includes current results and your approval tied to the profile. ColorChecker has its own section with patch names, reference and measured colours, and Delta E00. This is not automatic ISO certification. Two targets are not automatically combined; the current C2 verification provides the evidence.

title: Measure your already printed ColorChecker
lead: Select a saved verification target for the current ICC without creating or printing it again.
sections: 1. Select the target in step 9

Select C2. Save verification target as TIFF16 and click Run selected step. Choose Select existing target. The list shows saved targets in this project for the current ICC, with names, patch counts and folder IDs.
2. Match the physical print

Choose the ColorChecker entry matching your sheet. Example: Profile test ColorChecker-SG-D50-Lab | 153 patches. The count depends on the reference, repeats and any paper-white controls; not every ColorChecker target has 153 patches. Also compare the folder ID with your print file if several similar targets exist.
3. The saved print package is checked

InkProf checks ICC identity, TI2, manifest and TIFF16 patch values. The same saved print files are reused; no new layout or colour conversion is created. File checks do not prove that the physical print was made with the correct settings.
4. Begin measurement in step 10

Run C2. Measure / select verification revision and choose Measure. Confirm measurement target shows the target name and patch count. If they match your sheet, choose Measure this target, then Start measurement. Saved revisions is for measurements that are already saved.
5. Save and approve the result

Complete the measurement and choose Save and finish. Then run steps 11, 12, 13 and 14 for comparison, review, approval and certificate export. Changing the C2 target requires current results and a fresh approval; it does not change the ICC profile.
callout: If you printed both ColorChecker and a broader verification target, select the sheet you will measure first. Targets are measured separately. The certificate uses the current, measured and approved C2 target.

title: Study gradients through the ICC profile
lead: The external delivery folder includes test gradients and a screen preview through the delivered profile.
sections: Open the comparison

Open gradients.html beside the ICC, PDF and HTML certificate. Switch between Original and Soft proof. Select 100 % to inspect without scaling. The ramps include neutral, primary, secondary and blue-sky colours. These are generated test images; this feature does not open a custom JPG.
Which profile is used?

The soft proof uses the exact ICC included in the delivery. The original and preview JPGs contain embedded sRGB. Conversion uses relative colorimetric intent and black point compensation. gradients.json records settings and the profile SHA-256 identity.
Do InkProf profiles work?

InkProf profiles are normally expected to support this preview. The current printer profile checked during development worked. Not every possible profile variant has been tested, so this is not a guarantee for all profiles. A simplified profile used in automated code tests could not perform the conversion.
If the preview is unavailable

A profile may lack support for a colour conversion required by soft proof. The delivery is still saved and gradients.html explains that the preview could not be created. This does not automatically mean the profile is unsuitable for printing.
Save an updated delivery

Restart InkProf after updating and save an external delivery from step 14 again. Adding the JPGs alone does not require new measurements. Move the entire delivery folder to retain the comparison and report assets.
callout: Soft proof is the profile prediction on screen, not a physical measurement or approval. JPG is 8-bit and may introduce gradient steps itself. Inspect on a calibrated display and retain physical print verification.
